2611.08563.abstract: We present an analysis of the evolution of $[O\,III]+\mathrm{H}\beta$ equivalent width ($W_{\lambda}$) over the redshift range $z=3$ to $z=8.5$, based on combining the JWST NIRCam PRIMER and MINERVA imaging in the UDS survey field. We find that the combined medium- and broad-band data set reduces the photometric redshift outlier rate to $\eta = 4.7\%$ at $m_{\rm F444W}\leq28$, a $42\%$ reduction compared with PRIMER imaging alone. We also demonstrate that the combined data set facilitates the accurate recovery of $[O\,III]+\mathrm{H}\beta$ equivalent widths in redshift bins centred on $z\sim3.2,\, 4.0,\, 5.0,\, 7.2,\, 8.3$; corresponding to the F210M, F250M, F300M, F410M and F460M filters. Based on a final sample of $N=1964$ galaxies with $M_{\rm UV}\leq-19.25$, we first provide new constraints on the bright end of the $z=7-8$ $[O\,III]+\mathrm{H}\beta$ luminosity function ($\log_{10}\phi^{*} = -4.3_{-0.5}^{+0.2}$, $\log_{10}L^{*} = -43.4_{-0.2}^{+0.3}$), before proceeding to investigate the redshift evolution of $[O\,III]+\mathrm{H}\beta$ equivalent width. Using SED modelling based on non-parametric continuity star-formation histories, we find that the median $[O\,III]+\mathrm{H}\beta$ equivalent width monotonically increases with redshift, rising from $\mathrm{log}_{10}(W_{\lambda})=2.54^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$ at $z\simeq 3$ to $\mathrm{log}_{10}(W_{\lambda})=3.05^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$ at $z\simeq 8$. In tandem, the distribution of $\mathrm{log}_{10}(W_{\lambda})$ is observed to become increasingly asymmetric with redshift, producing a fraction of extreme emission-line galaxies (EELGs, $W_{\lambda}>1000\,$Å) that reaches $f_{\rm EELG}=0.50\pm{0.10}$ by $z=8.3$. Our SED modelling results indicate that the physical driver of this evolution is increasingly bursty star-formation, with EELGs the result of particularly high specific star-formation rates over the 10 Myr prior to observation.

2611.08594.abstract: Dust attenuation remains a dominant systematic uncertainty in measurements of an emission line, and therefore galaxies properties derived from the emission lines such as star formation rates. Corrections based only on the Balmer decrement require an assumed attenuation-curve slope, even though that slope varies among galaxies. We use JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from JADES to constrain effective dust attenuation curves for 386 star-forming galaxies at $0.5\leq z\leq7$. For each galaxy, we combine H$\alpha$, H$\beta$, and one additional hydrogen recombination line and solve for the normalization $\tau_V$ and slope $n$ of a power-law attenuation curve, allowing the slope to vary from galaxy to galaxy. We found slopes and normalization span a broad range even for galaxies at similar redshifts. Additionally, our method using Paschen transitions provided substantially greater constraints the attenuation-curve slope than Balmer-only combinations. When comparing to SMC-like or Calzetti-like corrections we find our method produces more consistent star formation rates with less scatter. These improved dust corrections provide an avenue to better describe star formation rates in the epoch of peak star formation and the early universe.

Multiple panels are used to illustrate different stages of the simulation and to capture its wide dynamic range. The panels show selected regions of the simulation at different spatial scales and evolutionary times. The top-left panel shows a dense gas filament in which stars have formed, with feedback from the newly formed stars evacuating the surrounding gas and producing an evacuated cavity. Star formation occurs along dense gas filaments and within molecular clouds. Protostellar jets are visible before the stars reach the main sequence (top right). The dashed red line is calculated by summing the progenitor counts of the sink particles in each snapshot, rather than counting the sink particles themselves. The progenitor count accounts for merger events that are not individually resolved, including numerical mergers and physically close systems that merge below the resolution limit (see Section II.2). Because some progenitors were never identified as separate sink particles in the stored snapshots, the red curve can exceed the cumulative number of unique sinks. The step-like behavior reflects discrete sink formation events over time.

Figure 4: Distribution of orbital properties for the bound pairs identified in binary and higher-order multiple systems in the simulation. For higher-order multiple systems, we calculate the orbital properties using the combined mass and center of mass of any inner bound pair.

Figure 5: Absolute radial velocity $v_{\rm rad}$ of stars as a function of physical distance from the halo center, at the time they each reach the main sequence or their highest protostellar stage if they do not reach the main sequence. The IMF includes all unique (proto)stars formed throughout the simulation, from $z\sim 16$ to $z\sim 7$, using their ZAMS masses or the maximum masses reached within their highest protostellar stages. Each panel corresponds to a unique halo and shows the IMF of its sink-particle population. The x-axis shows the time elapsed since each individual star formed, rather than the global simulation time. The color bar indicates the final stellar mass.

2611.08598.abstract: We present a cosmological radiation-magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) zoom-in simulation of $56$ Population III stars using FORGE'd in FIRE. Our simulation combines a cosmological initial condition centered on an isolated ultra-faint galaxy ($M_{\mathrm{halo}} \sim 10^9 M_\odot$ at $z=0$) with individual-star formation and feedback physics, reaching a maximum mass resolution of $\sim 10^{-2} M_\odot$ and spatial resolution of $\sim 10^{-3} \mathrm{pc}$. We follow continued star formation for just over $500$ Myr, from $z \sim 16$ to $z \sim 7$, substantially longer than what has been achieved before, and track star formation across five distinct minihalos. From our stellar population, we self-consistently resolve an emergent stellar initial mass function (IMF) and find $\alpha = 1.9$ for $dN/dM \propto M^{-\alpha}$ at $M_{\star} \gtrsim 2.2 M_{\odot}$. Additionally, we form both single and multiple stellar systems, including binaries and higher-order multiples, as well as stars with masses below $1 M_{\odot}$. At early times, the stellar mass distribution is more top-heavy, with a high-mass slope of $\alpha\sim1.4-1.5$, similar to previous Pop. III simulations, and steepens as star formation continues. This suggests that differences between our final IMF and previous studies may partly reflect the much longer evolution followed here, approximately five orders of magnitude longer than in several previous Pop. III sink-particle simulations. The first star-forming minihalo, which hosts the most massive stars in our simulation, has a shallower IMF slope of $\alpha\approx 1$, while later-forming minihalos produce lower maximum stellar masses in lower-density parent clouds.

2611.08599.title: Magnetically Arrested Accretion and Black Hole Spin in a Semi-Analytic Model of Galaxy Formation

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of the Mad Sage semi-analytic model structure showing the black hole growth channels, spin and mass evolution, AGN feedback modes, and gas reservoirs that govern galaxy formation within the model.

Figure 2: Stellar mass function at $z=0$ for all models explored in this work. The dashed crimson line shows the No-spin model, the orange line shows the Coherent only model, the blue line shows the Full-physics model, the green line shows the Full-physics + correction model, and the dotted pink line shows a run with AGN feedback turned off. Observational estimates from Baldry et al. [6], Bernardi et al. [13], and Driver et al. [39] are shown as grey squares, triangles, and diamonds, respectively. The Full-physics model overpredicts the number density of massive galaxies ($M_{\star}\gtrsim 10^{11}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$) relative to the No-spin model, encoding weaker AGN quenching. This served as motivation to include the $\eta_{\rm floor}$ correction. The Coherent only and Full-physics + correction model are in reasonable agreement with observations.

Figure 3: The $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\star}$ (left) and $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\rm bulge}$ (right) relations at $z=0$ for all models described in Table 1. The dashed crimson line shows the No-spin model, solid lines are the median relation for each spin model, and the shaded regions enclose the 68th percentile range. Observational data are shown as grey symbols: circles from Greene et al. [56], squares from Reines and Volonteri [114], and triangles from Sturm and Reines [143]. The right panel additionally includes data from Scott et al. [128]. The Full-physics models predict higher BH masses at fixed stellar mass than the No-spin model, while the Coherent only model shows the lowest BH masses. In the Coherent only model, coherent accretion drives spins to high values, raising the Novikov-Thorne radiative efficiency and reducing the fraction of accreted mass retained by the BH. Differences in the free parameter $\kappa_{\rm sink}$ between models may also contribute to the offset in BH masses at fixed stellar mass. All models remain broadly consistent with the observed scatter.

Figure 4: AGN energy density as a function of redshift for all models described in Table 1, decomposed into total energy output (left), jet power from radio-mode feedback (middle), and quasar-mode energy (right). Shaded bands show the 68th percentile bootstrap uncertainty from the simulation volume. The grey shaded region shows the observed kinetic energy density from radio-selected AGN compiled by Smolčić et al. [138], which represents an observational lower bound on the total jet power. The orange line shows the total kinetic density from the Serotina semi-analytic model [119]. All spin models predict lower total AGN energy densities than the No-spin model at $z\lesssim 5$. Among the spin models, the Full-physics + correction model produces slightly more energy output across all redshifts. This excess is driven by the self-consistent spin evolution combined with the minimum jet coupling enforced by $\eta_{\rm floor}$.

Figure 5: The AGN bolometric luminosity function from $z=0$ to $z=6$ for all our models. Observational data from Shen et al. [133] are shown in grey, compiled from multiple wavebands including rest-frame ultraviolet, B-band, soft and hard X-ray, and mid-infrared, with bolometric corrections applied. The dashed olive line shows Global fit A from Shen et al. [133]. At $z\geq 4$, additional data are included from Harikane et al. [60] ($4<z<7$), Maiolino et al. [84] ($4<z<11$), Matthee et al. [86] ($4.2<z<5.5$), and Kokorev et al. [76] ($4<z<9$). At $z=5-6$, the shaded red region shows the inferred luminosity function assuming that the Little Red Dots identified by JWST are AGNs [1], with further constraints from Greene et al. [55] ($z\geq 5$) and Guo et al. [57] ($z\sim 5$). The BH spin models remain mutually consistent across the full redshift range. The No-spin model overpredicts the AGN bolometric luminosity function at $z\gtrsim 4$, with its bright-end abundance more closely matching the JWST-inferred excess of luminous AGN. The BH spin models also overlap with the JWST constraints at those redshifts, but predict lower number densities that are more consistent with Shen et al. [133].

Figure 6: Stellar (top), H i (middle), and H2 (bottom) surface density profiles at $z=0$ for all our models. Dashed and solid lines show the median profile and shaded regions enclose the 68th percentile range across central galaxies with stellar mass $M_{\star}>10^{10}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, cold gas mass $M_{\rm cold}>10^{9.2}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, and bulge-to-total ratio $B/T<0.5$. Observed profiles of galaxies with similar properties from Leroy et al. [81] are shown in grey. All models broadly reproduce the observed surface density profiles at small radii ($r\lesssim 5\,\mathrm{kpc}$). At larger radii, the No-spin and Full-physics models predict more compact profiles than the Coherent only and Full-physics + correction models.

Figure 7: Left: Absolute magnitude of the BH spin as a function of BH mass for our Full-physics + correction model. The 2D histogram in gray shows the full population at $$z=0$$. Blue and red circles highlight actively accreting BHs ($f_{\rm Edd}>0.01$) with prograde ($a_{\star}\geq 0$) and retrograde ($a_{\star}<0$) spin respectively. The majority of prograde BHs cluster at $|a_{\star}|\sim 0.5$-$0.7$, while retrograde BHs have wide spread of high and low spin magnitudes. Blue squares with error bars show BH spin measurements from X-ray reflection spectroscopy compiled in Ricarte et al. [119]. Right: Median $|a_{\star}|-M_{\rm BH}$ relation from z=0 (dark blue) to $z=6$ (yellow), with shaded regions enclosing the 68th percentile range at each epoch. X-ray observations are shown for comparison. At low redshift, the median spin decreases with increasing BH mass. Massive BHs are systematically spun down by repeated episodes of Bondi accretion. At higher redshift ($z\gtrsim 3$), the median spin is broadly flat across BH mass, pointing to a regime in which cold disk feeding dominates BH growth at all masses.

Figure 8: BH mass-stellar mass relation colored by the median absolute BH spin at $z=0$ for our Full-physics + correction model. Each bin shows the median $|a_{\star}|$ for galaxies within that cell. The red solid line shows the median $M_{\rm BH}-M_{\star}$ relation, with dashed lines enclosing the 68th percentile ranges. At fixed BH mass, spin tends to decrease with increasing stellar mass, reflecting the shift from disk-fed accretion in low-mass galaxies towards incoherent Bondi accretion from the hot halo in more massive systems, where the Blandford-Znajek mechanism efficiently extracts spin energy to power the jet, and the BH-BH mergers with isotropically distributed progenitor spins further reduce or enhance the remnant spin magnitude.

Figure 9: Normalized BH spin distributions for our spin models compared against observations at $z=0$. Left: Distributions for BHs observable with X-ray reflection spectroscopy, selecting actively accreting BHs with $f_{\rm Edd}>0.01$. The black solid and dashed lines show the observed debiased and biased spin distributions compiled in Ricarte et al. [119]. The two Mad Sage models shown, the Coherent only model and the Full-physics + correction model, both predict spin distributions peaked at moderate values ($a_{\star}\sim 0.5$-$0.7$), falling short of both the biased and debiased observed distributions which peaks near $|a_{\star}|\approx 1$. Right: Distributions of BHs detected by the next-generation Event Horizon Telescope and/or the Black Hole Explorer, selecting massive, quiescent BHs with $M_{\rm BH}>10^{8}\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ and $f_{\rm Edd}<10^{-4}$. In both panels, the orange and green lines show our Coherent only and Full-physics + correction models respectively. Mad Sage models predict bimodal spin distributions for massive quiescent BHs, with populations at both moderate and low spin magnitudes driven by the balance between coherent disk feeding and prolonged ADAF-dominated spin-down.

Figure 10: Predicted LISA BH-BH merger event rates for three of our spin models, showing the cumulative event rate as a function of redshift (left), the differential event rate per logarithmic chirp mass interval (center), and the differential event rate per unit remnant spin magnitude (right). All rates are expressed per observer-frame year and include the $(1+z)^{-1}$ time-dilation correction. Events are selected within the LISA sensitivity band ($10^{4}\lesssim M_{\rm total}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\lesssim 10^{10}$, $z\leq 10$) using a SNR interpolation table. Mad Sage models all use the same TNG100-1 merger trees and a BH is seeded for every halo. Therefore, all three models produce nearly identical event rates as a function of redshift and chirp mass, since they share the same TNG100-1 merger trees and BH seeding prescription. The remnant spin distributions are indistinguishable between models, all peaking near $|a_{\star,\rm rem}|\approx 0.7$.

2611.08599.abstract: We present {\sc Mad Sage}, a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation that couples black hole mass and spin evolution to gas accretion and AGN feedback under magnetically arrested disk conditions. Building on the {\sc Dark Sage} model, we incorporate GRMHD-calibrated prescriptions for spin evolution and jet power, spin-dependent radiative efficiencies, and remnant spins from BH-BH mergers. We compare accretion and feedback models, including coherent disk-fed accretion with mixed coherent and incoherent hot-halo accretion, with and without additional mechanical feedback. We find that incoherent accretion, together with Blandford-Znajek spin-down, drives massive BHs toward low spins, reducing jet efficiencies and weakening the quenching of massive galaxies. Reproducing the high-mass end of the stellar mass function requires either exclusively coherent accretion or an additional feedback component provided by ADAF outflows. Our models broadly reproduce observed BH-galaxy scaling relations, disk surface density profiles, and the AGN luminosity function at $z\sim 2-6$, although the spin models under-predict the number density of faint AGN at low redshift. At $z\lesssim 3$, predicted BH spins decrease with increasing BH mass, while at higher redshifts, the mass dependence weakens. Spin distributions peak at $|a_\star|\sim 0.5$-$0.7$, below current X-ray reflection spectroscopy measurements, and become bimodal for massive, quiescent BHs accessible with the next generation Event Horizon Telescope and the Black Hole EXplorer. We report that the predicted LISA event rates are nearly independent of the adopted accretion and spin models.

2611.08603.abstract: We present a radiation-magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) cosmological zoom-in simulation of Pop III star formation, drawing initial conditions from a Milky Way-like progenitor halo at redshift $z \sim 21$. We follow the collapse of primordial gas over 10 orders of magnitude, through to the formation of an accretion disk that becomes gravitationally unstable $\Delta t \sim -3$ kyr before the first protostar's formation. Prominent spiral arms then develop and fragment vigorously, producing $\sim 60$ sink formation events over the first $8$ kyr post-collapse evolution, with a total stellar mass reaching $> 150\,{\rm M_\odot}$ by $15$ kyr, the end of our simulation. The disk remains magnetically supercritical throughout: the mass-to-flux ratio falls from $\mu_\Phi \sim 10^2$-$10^3$ to $\sim 15$ by $15$ kyr, as the inflow brings in magnetic flux. The magnetic energy in the disk remains sub-dominant throughout, but grows by $\sim 3.5$ orders of magnitude after the first star forms. The disk starts sub-virial and reaches virial equilibrium within $\sim 2$ kyr. The total stellar mass of the population grows as $M_* \propto t^2$, confirming the prediction of accelerating accretion in self-gravitating turbulent collapse, at rates of $\dot{M} \sim 10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}\,{\rm M}_\odot {\rm yr}^{-1}$. The star formation efficiency reaches $\approx 90\%$ within the disk (after $\approx 11$ kyr; $\approx 80\%$ at $9.5$ kyr) and $\sim 50\%$ within a $0.1$ pc sphere. We find a top heavy IMF ($dN/dm \propto m^{-\alpha}$) with a high-mass slope $\alpha \approx 1$. The cosmological environment sets the boundary conditions of the disk: an envelope delivers $\sim 3\times 10^{-3}\,{\rm M}_\odot {\rm yr}^{-1}$ to the outer edge of a disk with a radius of $\sim 10^{3}$ AU; the disk spreads and, in our simulation, its fragmentation sites move outward, from $\sim 500$ to $\sim 1350$\,AU, until it has been depleted.

2611.08612.abstract: We present dynamical masses for nine massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ from the JWST-IMFERNO program, measured from ultra-deep ($\sim32$hr), spatially resolved NIRSpec/MSA spectroscopy combined with NIRCam imaging. The most massive of these galaxies have previously been found to have a bottom-heavy initial mass function (IMF), based on measurements of dwarf-sensitive absorption features. Here, we examine whether the stellar masses inferred for these IMFs are consistent with the dynamical masses of these galaxies. We derive the dynamical masses by including Jeans Anisotropic Modelling within a forward-modelling framework that accounts for instrumental optics, source morphology, and geometric effects. We compare the resulting dynamical masses to the stellar masses for different IMF assumptions. A Milky Way IMF produces physically plausible dynamical-to-stellar mass ratios but implies central dark matter fractions ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.54\pm0.06$) that are a factor $\sim2$ higher compared to local ETGs and simulations. When uniformly applying the IMF that was measured from absorption features, the mean dark matter fraction becomes low ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.02\pm0.18$), and the stellar masses exceed the dynamical mass at $2\sigma$ significance for two out of seven galaxies in the sample. When we adopt the measured IMF only in the central $R_e$ and use a MW IMF in the outskirts, we find realistic dark matter fractions ($f_{\rm DM,1R_e}=0.28\pm0.12$) and consistent dynamical masses. These results support a scenario where the cores of the most massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ had a bottom-heavy IMF, similar to those observed in the centres of local early-type galaxies. Our results are consistent with an inside-out growth scenario, in which size and mass growth of massive galaxies proceeds after quenching through minor mergers, leaving the bottom-heavy cores mostly intact.

2611.08641.abstract: We analyze the gas kinematics in the proto-binary NGC 6334I(N) ALMAe9-ALMAe14 system with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 1.33 mm with an angular resolution of 66 mas (~90 au). With a separation of 740 au between the system members, these observations allow a detailed study of the gas motion around this likely binary system hosting at least one growing high-mass star. Some CH$_3$OH lines tracing cold gas ($E_u/k_B$~100 K) reveal the presence of ordered circumbinary gas motion around the binary system within a ~1000 au radius, and rotation around the individual sources with rotation axes pointing roughly in the same direction. We estimate a central source mass, uncorrected for inclination, of 2 M$_\odot$ for the secondary, while the primary has an estimated mass of 5 M$_\odot$ as reported in previous works. The CH$_3$OH transitions with higher $E_u/k_B$ ($\gtrsim400$ K) values reveal circumstellar gas rotation in ALMAe9 consistent with the cold gas tracers. The vibrationally excited SO emission also traces rotation around ALMAe9 and potentially an accretion shock from a flow feeding the circumstellar disk of ALMAe14. We identify two potential inflows feeding the circumstellar disks from the circumbinary gas at rates of ~$10^{-6}-10^{-4}$ M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ from CH$_3$OH emission. An additional third inflow seems to be feeding the primary from gas at larger scales.

2611.08648.abstract: We measure tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) distances to 17 dwarf satellites of M31 from Sloan $i$-band photometry of the Isaac Newton Telescope (INT) monitoring survey of Local Group dwarf galaxies, and add the distances of And I, And VII and And IX from earlier papers of the survey. We locate the tip with a Sobel edge-detection filter applied to the luminosity function of stars within two half-light radii of each galaxy. The distance moduli range from $23.38 \pm 0.06$ mag (And XVI, 474 kpc) to $25.35 \pm 0.06$ mag (And XVIII, 1177 kpc), and 15 of the 20 satellites lie between 650 and 850 kpc. For most galaxies, our distance agrees with at least one published value. Compared with Conn et al. (2012), our tip is brighter for 12 of the 18 galaxies in common, by up to 0.39 mag, possibly because of crowding in the central regions. And XII lies at $844^{+40}_{-38}$ kpc, about 60 kpc behind M31, consistent with a first infall into the Local Group. And XXII lies at $753^{+28}_{-27}$ kpc, closer than all earlier estimates, and about 59 kpc from M33 in three dimensions (for an M33 distance of 794 kpc), consistent with an association with M33. And XVIII lies about 400 kpc behind M31, too far for a secure association with M31.

2611.08828.abstract: AGN-driven outflows play a crucial role in regulating star formation in galaxies. These outflows are known to be multi-phase, and the characterization of the kinematics, extent, and energetics of each gas phase is needed to obtain a full picture of the outflow properties and impact. This study presents Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) integral field spectroscopy of the ionized gas outflow properties in seven low redshift (z<0.1) quasars---six Type 2 AGN and one narrow-line Type 1 AGN---providing insight into the warm ionized outflows in these luminous AGN. With the large field-of-view and high sensitivity of KCWI, these data reveal both larger ionized outflow extents than were previously known for these sources and uncover the existence of additional high-velocity kinematic components in the ionized outflows of these luminous AGN. We find (a) a high incidence (50-70%) of multiple outflows on scales of 4--10 kpc and (b) trends between the outflow extent, kinematics, and the ionized mass and energy outflow rates. These trends imply that the faster and often smaller outflows carry higher mass and energy outflow rates than the slower, larger outflows. We also find that the ionized gas outflows reach as far as the known extent of narrow-line ionized gas emission in AGN, which is known to depend weakly on AGN luminosity. This work highlights the utility of the current generation of wide-field integral field spectrographs on 8--10m class telescopes for studying quasar-driven outflows.

2611.08891.abstract: Context: HII regions are a key stage of massive star formation, where ionizing radiation reshapes the interstellar medium. Their continuum spectra trace thermal dust, free-free emission, and anomalous microwave emission (AME). Aims: We investigate how these components evolve as an HII region expands and correlate with gas and electron column densities across spatial scales. Methods: We post-process RAMSES radiation-magnetohydrodynamical simulations of a $10^4 M_\odot$ cloud with POLARIS. The model includes grain charging, rotational excitation and damping, radiative torques, rotational disruption, and emission from dust, ionized gas, and nano-composite grains. We compute maps and SEDs for six snapshots over $1-10^4$ GHz and analyze multi-scale correlations. Results: Ionized emission evolves from a compact, optically thick HII region to an extended, optically thin structure. Around 15 GHz, free-free emission changes from a $u^2$ to a $u^{-0.1}$ spectral regime as optical depth decreases, and increasingly traces electron column density. The thermal dust peak shifts from mid- to far-infrared as colder material contributes, while dust emission remains strongly correlated with total gas column density. AME peaks at 26-37 GHz and shows scale-dependent correlations with gas and electron distributions. Rotational disruption is the main dust-destruction mechanism affecting mid-infrared emission and the high-frequency AME tail. Conclusions: These continuum components provide complementary, scale-dependent diagnostics of stellar feedback. Self-consistent multi-frequency modeling is essential for interpreting surveys of star-forming clouds.

2611.08983.abstract: Identification of chemical substructures in the Galactic high-{\alpha} disk provides valuable insight into its formation history. In this work, we demonstrate the capability of low-resolution spectroscopy for this purpose by applying DBSCAN clustering to 87,275 red giants in the high-{\alpha} disk using 18 elemental abundances derived from LAMOST low-resolution spectra (R~1800). We assess the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the clustering results from the low-resolution data with those obtained by applying the same procedure to high-resolution survey abundances and to mock catalogs. These comparisons suggest that, despite the relatively large uncertainties in individual elemental abundances derived from low-resolution spectra, the astrophysical coherence among different elements provides sufficient information to identify chemically coherent families that may share similar enrichment histories without necessarily sharing a common birth environment. After scanning the parameter space of the DBSCAN procedure and merging the results from different parameter combinations, we identify 133 candidate chemical families containing 4,642 unique stars (5.3% of the high-{\alpha} disk sample). These families exhibit diverse multi-element abundance patterns, with particularly prominent differences in neutron-capture elements at nearly identical [Fe/H] values. These families therefore offer new constraints on the diversity of chemical enrichment pathways and on the assembly history of the high-{\alpha} disk.

2611.09044.abstract: Recent observational studies have identified phosphorus-rich (P-rich) stars ([P/Fe]>1.0) in both Galactic globular clusters (GCs) including three confirmed cases and the field population. Using analytical models of GC formation, we investigate a scenario in which P-rich stars form from pristine gas in GC-forming giant molecular clouds (GMCs) polluted by oxygen-neon (ONe) novae within and surrounding the GMCs. Within this framework, we model the chemical abundance patterns of P-rich stars using diverse chemical yield sets for ONe novae while varying the dilution factor (Fdil), defined as the ratio of pristine gas mass to total ONe nova ejecta mass. The principal results of our models are as follows: Across a wide range of Fdil, most models display positive correlations between [P/Fe], [N/Fe], [O/Fe], [Al/Fe]$, [Si/Fe], [S/Fe], and [Si/S]. The [Ce/Fe] ratios in P-rich stars can reach values up to 1 if the GMCs are additionally polluted by interacting low-mass asymptotic giant branch stars.P-rich star formation is highly unlikely in environments with a low interaction frequency between GMCs and ONe novae. P-rich stars exhibit anomalously low 14N/15N, 16O/17O, and 16O/18O isotopic ratios, offering a clear observational diagnostic to test this scenario. Assuming that P-rich Galactic field stars originate from GCs, we discuss the origin of their chemical abundance patterns. We suggest that the existence of P-rich stars provides direct evidence that GC-forming GMCs were polluted by pre-existing stellar populations.

2611.09086.abstract: We present SEDust, an automated pipeline for spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting and the estimation of stellar mass-loss and dust-production rates. We apply this pipeline to quantify the mass-loss and dust injection rates in the dwarf galaxy NGC~6822, focusing on long-period variables (LPVs) and pulsating asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars as major contributors to dust feedback into the interstellar medium. The total stellar mass-loss rate is found to be $(3.70 \pm 1.16) \times 10^{-3}\ M_{\odot} \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Two alternative methods (an LPV-based estimate and DESK) give totals that differ from this value by factors of $\sim$2.3 (lower) and $\sim$2.4 (higher), respectively, which we adopt as an estimate of the method-dependent systematic uncertainty. A positive correlation between stellar luminosity, intrinsic reddening caused by circumstellar dust self-extinction, and mass-loss rate is observed. The specific mass-return rate from AGB stars is $(7.40 \pm 2.30) \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, indicating that mass return from AGB stars alone is insufficient to sustain the current star formation rate of NGC~6822. This result implies the need for external gas accretion or additional mass-return mechanisms.

2611.09330.abstract: The large-scale structure (LSS) of the Universe shapes galaxy evolution through its intricate web-like morphology, yet its specific influence on gas-phase chemical abundances remains uncertain. Particularly, a homogeneous comparison of the N/O$-$O/H relation, a tracer of the mass assembly and baryonic cycle, across distinct LSS environments has been lacking. In this study, we analyse a local SDSS galaxy sample curated within the framework of the CAVITY project -- dedicated to studying void galaxies -- in which galaxies are classified by their LSS environment into three groups: clusters, voids, and non-cluster/non-void (NCNV). We extract spectroscopic emission line fluxes from the central SDSS spectra and analyse how different galaxy properties affect the scatter in the N/O$-$O/H relation. For that, we subtract the main N/O$-$O/H relation from the data and study the dependence of the resulting residuals ($\xi_\text{N/O}$) on a set of parameters, including stellar mass ($M_\star$), $g-r$ colour, and star formation rate (SFR). We find that $M_\star-$related variables are the best predictors of the scatter in the N/O$-$O/H relation, with little influence of the recent star formation history. Regarding the LSS comparison, no significant differences are found for void and NCNV galaxies. Cluster galaxies, however, present a N/O$-$O/H relation systematically lower (with $\xi_\text{N/O} \sim -0.02$). Consistent with this shift and with $M_\star$ as a good predictor of N/O$-$O/H deviations, we find that environmental dependences are also reflected in fundamental scaling relations: both the MZR and N/O$-M_\star$ relations are different for cluster galaxies. These combined results point to mechanisms in the dense intracluster medium (such as strangulation or re-accretion of metal-enriched gas) as the primary drivers of these chemical offsets for galaxies in cluster environments.

2611.09397.abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact sources with a blue rest-frame UV, a steep red optical continuum and, often, broad hydrogen lines. They have been interpreted as dense stellar systems, dust-reddened active galactic nuclei, or black holes embedded in dense, dust-poor gas, scenarios that are hard to tell apart in the rest-frame UV and optical. We present JWST/MIRI F770W and F1000W imaging of the triply lensed Abell2744-QSO1 at z=7.04, probing rest-frame 0.96 and 1.24um. QSO1 is unresolved, and its steep optical rise stops near rest-frame 1um. Up to 1.24um, a T~4450K blackbody, or a hotter one reddened by dust, describes the continuum, with no sign of the hot dust seen in most type-1 quasars. Our statistically preferred SED fits produce the red continuum with (3-4)x10^9 Msun of stars, over 100 times the dynamical limit on the host mass, and are therefore disfavoured. An accretion disc in a dense gas cocoon respects this limit but over-predicts the 1.24um flux by 5 sigma. Super-Eddington accretion models with a thermalising envelope reproduce the turnover, but only for a black hole ~2.5dex less massive than the dynamical estimate. For a dust-reddened accretion disc (A_V ~ 2 mag), dust at ~1200K can re-emit at most ~2 per cent of the absorbed luminosity, and most of it would have to emerge at ~70-600K, unless the dust covers only a small fraction of the sky. The dynamics favour an accretion-powered source, but our data cannot distinguish dust reddening from processing by dense gas. MIRI imaging at >18um could separate these scenarios.

2611.09531.abstract: Collisionless self-gravitating systems, such as merging galaxies, have long seemed an exception to the statistical-mechanical principle that chaotic many-body systems relax to maximum-entropy states: Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of their "violent relaxation," constrained by exact conservation of phase-space volume -- equivalently, of infinitely many collisionless "Casimir" invariants -- has appeared not to be a good description. We propose that violent relaxation does give rise to Lynden-Bell's maximum-entropy equilibria, but that both are underpinned by gravitational turbulence, in which large-scale gravitational fluctuations drive chaotic phase-space mixing of the particles' distribution function. We derive the universal small-scale (sub-Jeans) spectra of this turbulence and show that it leads to phase-space-volume conservation being broken on a timescale only logarithmically longer, in the particle number N, than the dynamical (violent-relaxation) time. This timescale separation lets the system relax "adiabatically" through a sequence of Lynden-Bell equilibria, each corresponding to instantaneous values of the Casimirs. At long times, it approaches an equilibrium close to its "ground state": a distribution whose Casimirs have adjusted so that the system's energy is now its minimum possible energy. Thus, the system's universal tendency is toward a minimum-energy, maximum-entropy state. We corroborate this picture with 1D N-body simulations and hypothesize that it can explain the universal equilibria of galaxies and dark-matter halos.

2611.09852.abstract: Cosmological simulations within the standard cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm systematically predict higher values of the dimensionless bar-speed parameter, $\boldsymbol{R} \equiv R_{\mathrm{cr}}/R_{\mathrm{bar}}$ (where $R_{\mathrm{cr}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{bar}}$ denote the corotation radius and the bar radius, respectively), than those inferred from observations of local galaxies, a discrepancy known as the fast-bar tension. Since bar slowdown is primarily driven by dynamical friction with the dark matter halo, bar dynamics is inherently sensitive to the properties of dark matter particles. We aim to determine whether dark matter self-interactions alleviate or exacerbate the fast-bar tension, and to identify the physical mechanism behind the differences in bar dynamics between CDM and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models. We use the $51.7\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ box of the AIDA-TNG cosmological simulations, run with three different dark matter models: standard CDM, and two SIMD models one with a constant cross-section model (SIDM1), and the other with a velocity-dependent model (vSIDM). We identify barred disk galaxies with stellar mass $M_* > 10^{10}\,M_{\odot}$ at redshifts $z=0.2,\,1.0,\,1.5,$ and $2.0$, and measure the bar fraction, bar strength, bar length, pattern speed $\Omega_{\mathrm{p}}$, and the ratio $\boldsymbol{R}=R_{\mathrm{cr}}/R_{\mathrm{bar}}$. The pattern speeds in the SIDM1 and vSIDM models are generally lower than in CDM at nearly all redshifts probed in this study. The subsequent slowdown proceeds with nearly 10\% more effective in the SIDM models likely due to velocity-anisotropy. Consequently, at low redshift the mean value of $\boldsymbol{R}$ is significantly higher in the SIDM models, indicating that the fas-bar tension is further exacerbated in these scenarios.

2611.09871.abstract: We present high-angular and velocity resolution observations of the emission lines of [CII] at 158 micron, [CI] at 609 micron, and the 12CO and 13CO (J=3-2) transitions toward the central region of NGC 6334, providing a detailed multi-phase view of carbon in this massive star-forming complex. By combining morphology and spatial scales information, kinematics, line profiles, and line ratio analyses, we quantify the distribution and physical state of ionized and atomic carbon, and carbon in its molecular form in CO. [CII] emission is the most extended, permeates the mapped region and is dynamically complex, while 13CO is compact and quiescent, and 12CO and [CI] occupy intermediate regimes connecting dense regions to transitional diffuse layers. We interpret these emission distributions such that the brightest [CII] emission traces photodissociation regions (PDRs) close to the H II region bubbles located along the central filament, while the extended [CII] emission arises from the more diffuse warm gas, indicating either cloud formation or dispersal processes. Remarkably, the [CI] is more extended than the 13CO, but less than [CII] and may probe the gas velocity structure resulting from colliding flows or cloud-cloud collisions. Line ratios involving [CII], such as [CII]/[CI] or [CII]/CO are systematically high, revealing widespread diffuse emission and localized UV-illuminated surfaces. Line ratio analysis and K-means clustering of [CI]/13CO versus dust continuum (cold 870 micron and warm 70 micron) emission reveal stratified chemical structure that UV photons penetrate deeply into the clumpy ridge (Av~18), suggesting a porous PDR. These results together depict that NGC 6334 is a clumpy, feedback-dominated PDR ridge with coexisting carbon phases, where [CI] and [CII] also trace dynamical processing through multiple velocity components linked to cloud-cloud collisions.

2611.09875.abstract: SN 2026ahvu is a Type Ia supernova (SN) that occurred in the nearby galaxy NGC 1433. Using archival Hubble and JWST imaging from the PHANGS survey, we show that the SN lies within 0.19$''$ and 0.26$''$ of two UV-bright star clusters. This $0.19/0.26''$ separation corresponds to $8/11$ pc ($17/24$ pc) at the reported distances of $9.1$ and $18.9$ Mpc, respectively. The probability of finding an unrelated Type Ia SN this close to a cataloged star cluster by chance is only $\sim$0.4 %. Thus, SN 2026ahvu is likely the first Type Ia SN that can be associated with relatively young star clusters in a nearby galaxy. From spectral energy distribution fitting using HST+JWST (or HST-only) data, we find that the clusters have age estimates of $37_{-5}^{+3}$ ($57_{-9}^{+14}$) Myr and $95_{-13}^{+15}$ ($88_{-12}^{+14}$) Myr. Association with either cluster would mean that SN 2026ahvu should be considered a prompt SN Ia and provide one of the most concrete measurements to date of a prompt Ia delay time. The median age of the younger star cluster is close to the minimum possible delay time for SN Ia progenitors. If the SN is indeed associated with the younger cluster, it would imply that Type Ia SNe can occur almost immediately after white dwarf formation. If the SN is associated with the older cluster, this discovery still presents the first example of a prompt Type Ia SN with delay time under 100 Myr.

2611.08676.abstract: There are exceedingly few chemical abundance measurements available in the literature for K dwarf stars, especially for those with T$_{eff} <$ 4700 K due to an incompatibility of traditional analyses with their molecular-line-ridden optical spectra. To address the need for K dwarf abundance constraints, we present an elemental ([C/H], [O/H]) and isotopic ($^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O) abundance analysis for six K dwarf exoplanet host stars: K2-141, NGTS-10, WASP-43, WASP-69, WASP-80, and HATS-72. Each system hosts an exoplanet targeted by JWST characterization efforts, making host star abundances especially critical as baseline references. Using MARCS model atmospheres, the TurboSpectrum spectral synthesis code, and near-infrared IGRINS spectra, we derive novel [C/H] and [O/H] abundance ratios for these high-priority K dwarf host stars. We further investigate prospects for determining $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C and $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios using $^{13}$C$^{16}$O and $^{12}$C$^{18}$O lines from the 2.3 micron CO bandhead. The observed spectra are too noisy to measure $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios for the sample, but we do find sub-solar $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratios for five out of six targets. We also derive uniform gyrochronological ages for each host star to compare with galactic chemical evolution models and identify underlying abundance-age trends. NIR H+K band spectroscopy provides an alternative to optical, atomic line-derived carbon and oxygen abundances for cool dwarf stars. The growing catalog of precise host star elemental and isotopic abundances complements ongoing observations of their companions and provides a baseline for understanding their chemical composition, origin, and evolution.

2611.08847.abstract: Abell 2744 (Pandora's Cluster) is a massive galaxy cluster undergoing multiple mergers, characterized by a highly disturbed X-ray morphology, elevated intracluster medium (ICM) temperatures, and several radio relics associated with merger driven shocks. We present NuSTAR observations of Abell 2744 aimed at mapping its thermodynamic structure and constraining the presence of inverse Compton (IC) scattering from relativistic electrons. We measure the temperature distribution across the cluster and identify a prominent shock front with a Mach number of $\mathcal{M} = 1.58^{+0.42}_{-0.30}$, aligning with the southeastern boundary of the radio halo. The global NuSTAR spectra are modeled with single- and two-temperature thermal components, as well as thermal plus power-law models to test for IC emission. The spectra are well described by purely thermal models with an average temperature of $kT \approx 11$ keV, and we find no significant evidence for non-thermal hard X-ray emission. We derive a 90\% confidence upper limit on the $20-80$ keV IC flux of $ F_{\rm nt} < 2.31 \times 10^{-12} erg~s^{-1}~cm^{-2}$. Combining this with 1.5 GHz diffuse radio measurements from the VLA, we estimate a lower limit on the average magnetic field strength of $B > 0.2 \ \rm{\mu G}$.

2611.08925.abstract: Extended main-sequence turn-offs (eMSTOs) observed in open clusters younger than $2~\mathrm{Gyr}$ are commonly attributed to a spread in stellar rotation rates. Tidal synchronization in close binary systems has been proposed as a possible mechanism for producing slowly rotating stars. To test this hypothesis, we measured the radial-velocity (RV) dispersions of slow-rotator samples associated with the eMSTOs of eight open clusters using ESO VLT/GIRAFFE and SALT/RSS spectroscopy. We extended the analysis to 40 open clusters using Gaia DR3 RV measurements. The observed cluster RV dispersions are generally substantially smaller than those predicted for binary populations dominated by close systems with orbital periods for which tidal synchronization is expected to be effective. In particular, all 40 clusters in the Gaia sample have RV dispersions below the prediction of the $P=10$ d binary-population model. These results suggest that close, tidally synchronized binaries are unlikely to be the dominant origin of slow-rotator populations in young and intermediate-age open clusters, although a contribution from undetected or wider binary systems cannot be excluded.

2611.09039.abstract: Gaia has discovered dormant compact-object binaries in which the compact object shows no observable interaction with its luminous companion. These systems, hereafter Gaia BHs and Gaia NSs for black hole (BH) and neutron star (NS) companions, provide a new probe of compact-object binary formation. These detached systems are difficult to produce through standard isolated binary evolution alone, and their formation pathways remain unclear. Previous $N$-body studies have shown that Gaia BH-like objects are formed efficiently in star clusters, while Gaia NS-like objects are not. This has been attributed to the BH subsystem dominating the cluster core. We performed direct $N$-body simulations of $10^4 \mathrm{M}_\odot$ star clusters in a Galactic tidal field and investigated how NS-main-sequence (NS-MS) binaries form during the late BH-depleted phase. We found that NS-MS binaries satisfying Gaia-sensitive criteria form only after BH depletion. NSs are present in the core throughout the evolution, but the strong encounters there are monopolized by the BH subsystem until it is depleted. Our results show that the dynamical formation of Gaia-sensitive NS-MS systems is not prevented in star clusters, but delayed relative to Gaia BH-like systems.

2611.09308.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) photodesorption regulates the partitioning of water between interstellar ice mantles and the gas phase, yet laboratory yields are generally measured on planar substrates rather than on surfaces representative of cosmic dust. We investigate how grain morphology affects UV photodesorption from thin H$_2$O ice films of 2-6 monolayers deposited on planar gold and olivine, soot nanoparticles, and olivine microparticles. Samples were irradiated at 12 and 60 K with a microwave-discharge hydrogen lamp, and ice depletion was monitored by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and reflection-absorption infrared spectroscopy. On planar gold, the photodesorption yield increases approximately linearly with ice coverage, from $\sim5\times10^{-4}$ to $\sim2\times10^{-3}$ molecule photon$^{-1}$ between 2 and 6 monolayers, consistent with increasing UV absorption in optically thin ice; planar olivine gives comparable yields. In contrast, photodesorption is suppressed on particulate olivine and, more strongly, on soot, where yields are up to a factor of $\sim40$ lower than on gold at 12 K. Both experimental techniques confirm the strong suppression of ice depletion on soot. These results show that UV photodesorption depends not only on ice coverage but also strongly on grain morphology. The pronounced suppression on soot may reflect heterogeneous ice growth and altered energy redistribution within nanoscale ice domains, implying that yields measured on planar substrates may substantially overestimate photodesorption from the thin ice mantles of cosmic dust.

2611.09546.abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes can become extremely dense following gravothermal core collapse, motivating their use as explanations for unusually concentrated gravitational lenses. Using an emulator calibrated on gravothermal fluid calculations, we investigate whether increasing central density necessarily strengthens lensing. We follow initially Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) haloes through core formation and collapse deep into the short-mean-free-path regime, and compute finite-source magnifications, critical curves, and source-plane lensing cross sections for isolated spherical haloes with elastic, velocity-independent self-interactions, including external shear in selected calculations. Lensing strength evolves non-monotonically: it initially decreases during core formation, rises during early collapse, and generally declines at later stages despite continued growth of the central density. This decline accompanies the emergence of a dense inner core whose mass and radius decrease within a more extended, lower-density core. Time-averaged enhancement relative to NFW haloes depends on the lensing statistic, halo concentration, and interaction cross section. Generalized NFW haloes with central cusps $\rho \propto r^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma \geq 2$ always have larger lensing efficacies than core-collapsed SIDM haloes of equal mass and are therefore poor proxies, including in terms of the demographics (size and radial thickness) of arcs and Einstein rings. The core collapse stage at which SIDM haloes are optimal lenses coincides with the epoch at which the characteristic core surface density is close to critical, which typically occurs during the early stages of core collapse. These results demonstrate that central density alone is insufficient to characterize SIDM lensing and that its evolving mass distribution must be modelled explicitly.

2611.09588.abstract: Molecular outflows probe protostellar accretion and mass transfer from clump scales to forming stars. We present an ALMA study of CO (J=2-1) outflows toward 13 massive clumps from the SQUALO sample, spanning a broad evolutionary range and exhibiting clump-scale infall. We identify 51 high-velocity CO lobes associated with 31 outflow systems and derive their physical and dynamical properties assuming local thermodynamic equilibrium. Outflow inferred accretion rates are typically 10^{-5}-10^{-3} Msun/yr, consistent with active massive star formation. The maximum outflow velocity shows little dependence on candidate driving-core mass, indicating that it is not a reliable tracer of protostellar mass in clustered environments. Outflow momentum flux correlates positively with clump surface density, whereas accretion rate shows a tentative, statistically nonsignificant decrease with increasing virial parameter. Total outflow inferred accretion rate shows a tentative positive relation with clump-scale infall rate but remains systematically lower, suggesting that the detected outflows represent only part of the large-scale mass flux. The clump L/M ratio moderately anticorrelates with projected outflow length, although projection, observational limitations, and the embedded source population prevent a unique evolutionary interpretation. Together with the continuum derived fragmentation properties, our results show that compact cores embedded within infalling clumps drive the outflows. The tentative relation between clump-scale infall and protostellar accretion suggests a possible connection across these scales, although our observations do not directly trace mass transfer from filaments to individual protostars.

2611.09720.abstract: A radio/X-ray Fundamental Plane (FP) test of an intermediate-mass black hole is informative only when the compact radio emission, hard X-rays, accretion state, and host association refer to the same accretor. We used published VLA, VLBA, \textit{Chandra}, and \textit{HST} observations of a radio-selected dwarf-galaxy sample to determine when present nondetections are constraining and what observations are required for a stronger test. The VLBA follow-up reveals that compactness alone does not establish association with the target dwarf, while for the best nuclear candidates the radio component relevant to the FP has not yet been isolated on the intermediate physical scales between the VLA and VLBA measurements. We therefore recast the FP as a forward question: for an assumed black-hole mass, how likely is a given radio observation to detect the compact core? The calculation includes intrinsic FP scatter, X-ray uncertainties, the radio spectral index, the accretion state, and source size relative to the beam. The existing VLBA nondetections have low completeness across the adopted intermediate-mass range and do not provide useful black-hole mass upper limits. Meaningful tests require deeper resolution-matched radio imaging, recovery of intermediate-scale structure, and contemporaneous measurements of the intrinsic hard-X-ray component. Because the calculation returns a mass-dependent detection function for each source, the same framework can be applied to larger dwarf-galaxy samples to quantify survey completeness and build selection functions for population studies of low-mass black holes.
